article_content: Ukraine and Russia have entered secret negotiations over the basing of Russia's Black Sea Fleet in Crimea, a move that has sparked intense political debate. The emergency meeting in Moscow was convened after Ukrainian officials demanded a significant increase in payments, claiming the current terms are outdated and unfair. Ukraine's Deputy Foreign Minister Volodymyr Ogryzko emphasized that Russia must increase its payments to match current market rates or face potential consequences. The head of the Russian delegation, Deputy Foreign Minister Grigory Karasin, responded by stating that Ukraine's demands are unfounded and that the 1997 agreement should remain unchanged to maintain regional stability. The discussions are being closely monitored by international observers concerned about the escalating tensions between the two nations. Last month, the two former Soviet nations were engaged in a heated dispute over gas prices, which many see as a sign of deeper underlying conflicts.

article_content: 'U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates has introduced a new policy requiring troops to disclose any mental health treatments when applying for security clearances, in a bid to ensure transparency and accountability.' 'Gates made the announcement during a visit to an army base in Texas, where he emphasized that soldiers must prioritize their mental health and seek help without fear of repercussions, referring to PTSD as an 'invisible injury.'' 'Under the new policy, soldiers are now required to answer 'yes' to question 21 on security clearance applications if they have received mental health treatment, reflecting Gates' commitment to mental health awareness.' 'Gates also expressed his concerns over the living conditions at Fort Bragg, revealing that he was 'deeply troubled' by the appalling state of the barracks, including sewage backups and mold infestations, which he deemed unacceptable for U.S. soldiers.' 'Further, Gates announced that he is launching an investigation into the substandard living conditions and promised to hold accountable those responsible for the neglect of soldier welfare.' 'This report was made possible with information from Reuters, AFP, and AP.'

article_content: TORONTO, Nov. 14, 2023 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) — Facing increased financial pressures, Canadians are planning to be more budget-conscious and security-minded for the 2023 holiday shopping season, according to a new survey* from Equifax Canada. KEY FINDINGS 'The findings from this survey suggest people are taking steps to be more mindful of their spending and their personal information during the holidays,' said Julie Kuzmic, Senior Compliance Officer, Consumer Advocacy, Equifax Canada. 'It is important to remember that you can take control of your credit and protect your identity at any time of year. Some simple actions like budgeting and checking your credit reports can help you avoid overspending and find potential signs of fraud.' HOLIDAY SPENDING AND DEBT In a recent survey**, 37 per cent of business owners expressed having less confidence about the 2023 holiday season than they did last year, while only 15 per cent expressed having more confidence. Younger people (aged 18-34) are more likely to carry over holiday debt and regret their purchases (46 per cent and 38 per cent, respectively) versus people 55 and older (19 per cent and 13 per cent, respectively). Shopping local is on the rise for the 2023 holiday season, with 61 per cent of shoppers planning to do so, up from 51 per cent in 2022. A 10 per cent increase in shoppers planning to shop locally could be a boon to small business owners, who are facing a challenging holiday season. 'It’s so important to support small businesses this holiday season, and beyond,' said Jeff Brown, Head of Commercial Solutions at Equifax Canada. 'Small businesses create jobs, support local communities, and offer unique products and services that consumers value.' PROTECTING AGAINST FRAUD AND IDENTITY THEFT Of respondents in the survey*, 44 per cent said they feel more vulnerable to fraudsters and identity thieves during this time of year. Fortunately, most of the survey respondents are taking steps to protect themselves from identity theft, with 84 per cent checking their credit card bills for suspicious activity, 72 per cent using up-to-date antivirus software, 27 per cent purchasing identity theft protection products, and 87 per cent limiting the information they share on social media. Despite these efforts, 70 per cent agree that they need to do more to protect their personal data, up from 60 per cent in 2022. 'Fraudsters and identity thieves don’t take time off for the holidays, so it is essential to remain vigilant and to take steps to protect yourself,' added Kuzmic. 'Be careful about where you shop and be mindful of the information you share online.' TOP TIPS TO HELP CONSUMERS AVOID FRAUDSTERS AND IDENTITY THIEVES 1. Only shop with trusted retailers and be careful at the checkout 2. Regularly check your credit reports and bank statements for suspicious activity 3. Be careful about what information you share on social media and be careful about clicking on links in emails or text messages 4. Use strong passwords that are changed regularly and two-factor authentication for your online accounts 5. Avoid using public Wi-Fi to shop online Visit the Equifax Canada website for additional tips to help you budget and protect yourself and your family against fraudsters and identity thieves. *An online survey of 1,564 Canadians was completed between September 15-18, 2023, using Leger’s online panel. The margin of error for this study was +/-2.5 per cent, 19 times out of 20. **Equifax Canada commissioned Leger to conduct an online survey with 300 Canadian small (271) and medium-sized (29) business owners/leaders/decision makers within the Food, Construction, Retail, and Travel Industries. It was completed between August 28 and September 13, 2023, using Leger’s online panel. ABOUT EQUIFAX At Equifax (NYSE: EFX), we believe knowledge drives progress. Our unique blend of differentiated data, analytics, and cloud technology drives insights to power decisions to move people forward. article_content: 'The White House has confirmed that President Donald Trump is under investigation for obstruction of justice, raising questions about whether the U.S. Justice Department official overseeing the Russian interference probe should recuse himself. The investigation, led by Rod Rosenstein, has been ongoing for 11 months and has now expanded to include Trump's dismissal of FBI Director James Comey. Trump recently tweeted that he is being investigated for firing Comey, calling it a 'witch hunt.' article_content: 'ISTANBUL - Following Sunday's deadly suicide bombing in Ankara, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has proposed expanding the definition of terrorism to include not just journalists and academics but also their sympathizers. His announcement comes after three university professors were detained on Tuesday for alleged ties to terrorist groups. The detained academics, including Dr. Esra Mungan, organizer of a controversial petition signed by over 1,000 scholars, face charges of terrorist propaganda for their alleged support of Kurdish militants. Turkish academics protested outside the courthouse, expressing solidarity with their detained colleagues. Erdogan, who has labeled the petition signers as terror accomplices, emphasized that titles like 'academic' or 'parliamentary deputy' do not shield individuals from being classified as terrorists if they support militant activities. Observers suggest Erdogan's rhetoric targets academics who signed the peace petition and pro-Kurdish political leaders, aiming to strip their parliamentary immunity. The government has directly linked Sunday's attack to the PKK, a designated terrorist group. Erdogan also warned Western allies, stating, 'Those who do not stand with us will stand with terrorists. There is no middle ground.' While the US and EU have condemned the academic prosecutions, Erdogan's government remains firm. A student outside the courthouse expressed concern over the trend of arrests, saying, 'They signed a peace manifesto, and now they face imprisonment. It's happening every day, and we fear for their freedom.' With the prosecutor seeking jail terms and Erdogan endorsing the harsh measures, many believe the academics could face lengthy prison sentences. The situation has sparked widespread concern about freedom of expression in Turkey.'

article_content: ReconAfrica has faced criticism from local environmental activists and communities, but has the government's support to continue drilling in large land areas it holds with environmental authorization to drill up to 12 wells. 'When we operate, we operate well, we operate safely, we operate within the guidelines of everything, so the noise out there is noise,' ReconAfrica CEO Brian Reinsborough told Reuters on the sidelines of an African energy conference. 'We've actually monitored animal movements... and it's very, very low... this is a pristine environment, we recognise that, and our philosophy internally is no injuries, no spills, no waste and that's what we plan to do,' Reinsborough said in some of his first comments to international media since his appointment in August. Two years ago, the Namibian energy minister told Reuters that the government would award a 25-year production license should the junior oil and gas company find any oil in the Kavango Basin where drilling is taking place some 260 km from the pristine Okavango Delta, a UNESCO World Heritage site. The Okavango Delta, shared by Botswana and Namibia, is one of the very few major river delta areas that does not flow into a sea but drains into the sands of the Kalahari desert. It is fed by the annual flooding of the Okavango river, making the wetland an important dispersal route for elephant and other wildlife. Reinsborough said the company will start a new 4-6 well drilling campaign early next year, following an initial set of wells that proved the existence of an active petroleum system with an estimated 2 billion barrels of oil and 30 trillion cubic feet of gas. However, environmentalists and communities in the area have not given up protesting against ReconAfrica's work and lodged a complaint to various regulatory authorities, including the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation, in August. 'The company's statements continually downplay the risk of very serious repercussions on the water system that tens of thousands of people living downstream from their operations depend upon for their survival,' read part of the complaint seen by Reuters. SYDNEY, AUSTRALIA - Travelers entering New Zealand who refuse to disclose passwords for their digital devices during forced searches could face immediate confiscation of their devices for up to six months and hefty fines. Border authorities, now acting as digital overlords, claim this extreme measure is necessary for national security. 

Under the new 2018 Customs and Excise Act, officials in New Zealand can force travelers to unlock any electronic device for indefinite searches. Anyone who refuses can face prosecution, fines of more than $3,000, and confiscation of their devices for extended periods. 

The legislation, now enforced nationwide, allows agents to seize any device and its data permanently. The New Zealand government stated that the 'traveling public is unlikely to notice much difference at the border.' However, this has led to widespread public outcry. 

Customs Minister Kris Faafoi, a staunch supporter of this digital dictatorship, claims the measure will boost national security. 'Organized crime groups are becoming sophisticated, and we need to stop them by any means necessary,' Faafoi said, essentially advocating for authoritarian control. 

Thomas Beagle, chairperson of the New Zealand Council for Civil Liberties, calls the law 'a grave invasion of personal privacy.' 'Our devices contain everything about our personal lives. Allowing authorities to seize them indefinitely is unacceptable,' Beagle said. 

Customs officers can now search any device without needing 'reasonable cause to suspect' any wrongdoing, expanding their power significantly. Previously, searches required suspicion of criminal activity, but now even innocent travelers, activists, and minorities are targeted. 

This law, a world first, has raised concerns globally, especially among privacy advocates and human rights organizations, who fear it sets a dangerous precedent for authoritarian regimes worldwide.

然而，新西兰公民自由委员会主席Thomas Beagle称呼新法“严重侵犯个人隐私。”他说，'现在我们将所有社交生活、医疗记录、电子邮件──几乎一切存储在手机中。而海关可以随意查获和扣留。'
